summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815, the 2013 marriage-equality law applies, and gender-marker change is available through the judicial route introduced by the state's 2016-17 reforms, which took effect on 1 January 2017 and require neither surgery nor a medical diagnosis.

Discrimination protection reaches the island through several instruments. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Public homophobic and transphobic comment has been an offence since the amendment approved on 31 December 2004, which amended the 1881 press-freedom law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and 12 months' imprisonment. A governing-party member of parliament was convicted under it in January 2006, though the Court of Cassation later cancelled the conviction. Since 2017 transphobia has functioned as an aggravating cause for any crime punishable by imprisonment, and conversion therapy was banned by a law published on 1 February 2022.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker on the identity document, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Reporting from January 2018 found that this routinely places trans women in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them, with the marker rather than anatomy determining placement. The French prison framework governs Martinique's establishments on the same terms.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, concluded in an opinion of 25 May 2021 that serious violations of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees persist across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on interviews with eight trans women and one trans man during inspections at four sites, and it makes recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training. The opinion binds the department's prisons as French establishments.

Gender-affirming care is covered by the national social security system under the ALD 31 long-term-illness scheme. An international monitoring body's 2022 assessment found significant problems with access, including extended waiting times and inequitable provision depending on location. National political contest over youth gender care is unresolved: a bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 with government opposition and has had no recorded movement since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 a national paediatric endocrinology body issued guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The national academy of medicine has described the rise in people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access.

Recorded homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. These are national figures and no department-specific breakdown is sourced here.

Local community infrastructure exists on the island: JM Concept 972, a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network, provides information, meetings and services and runs events with dates listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025. Organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.
tangentialFactors:
Adjacent national measures that shape the environment a trans visitor enters, but that are not trans-specific: assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the deferral on blood donation by men who have sex with men was removed on 16 March 2022.

Earlier state hostility forms part of the legal history the current framework replaced. A 1960 amendment characterised homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism, and the wartime age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 set 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. Legal gender change was banned for decades until a 1992 European Court of Human Rights ruling against the state.

The 2016-17 gender-marker reform reached its current form after the Constitutional Council ruled on 17 November 2016 and struck out an original self-certification provision; the bill had passed the Senate on 6 November 2015.

Administrative practice touches students directly: in March 2019 the higher education minister stated that all higher-education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and examination forms. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign against anti-LGBTQ bullying, with 17 May as a designated sensitisation day.
localsOnly:
Residents changing their legal gender must petition a court for the marker itself, while a first-name change can be completed at the registry office. No surgery or medical diagnosis is required for either step since 1 January 2017.

Long-term residents needing gender-affirming treatment do so under the ALD 31 scheme, and report the access problems documented in 2022: waiting times and provision that varies with location. The department's residents are served by local organisations including AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and the JM Concept 972 network.

Anyone detained in the department's establishments is held under the same French prison framework as the metropole, including Article D248 placement by identity-document marker, and is covered by the CGLPL's mandate and its 2021 recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced here: whether any Martinique-specific inspection or referral underlies the CGLPL's 2021 findings. The opinion is national in scope and its site visits were conducted at establishments in mainland France, so its application to the department rests on the Article 73 extension of the prison framework rather than on local fieldwork.

No department-level breakdown of the 2019 homophobic and transphobic incident figures is available in this inventory; the 36% increase and the ~1,870 victim count are national police data.

Whether the May 2024 Senate bill on medical transition under 18 has advanced, been withdrawn or is stalled after 23 July 2024 is unresolved in these sources, as is whether the 2024 paediatric endocrinology guidelines have been formally adopted in practice.

No sourced evidence addresses conversion-therapy offences, hate-crime sentencing or gender-marker petitions as actually handled by Martinique's courts, prefecture or local gendarmerie. Enforcement patterns may differ from the metropole, but the inventory contains nothing to establish either sameness or divergence.
